I was involved with this project as a reporter, though others from my organisation did most of the work.HN readers may be interested to know a bit about the tech stack. The 15 million or so documents, mostly Outlook mailbox exports, were provided to partners in the consortium via a tool called OpenAleph [1], which is maintained by DARC and based on ElasticSearch and a schema called FollowTheMoney [2], developed specifically for the investigative journalism use case. A lot of the original work on this was done by Friedrich Lindenberg (@pudo), who now runs OpenSanctions [3].The timing was v. interesting given where we are with LLMs -- it's the first major leak I've worked on where it was possible to leverage local models to do some of the heavy lifting, and this only got more possible as the project went on. The coordinators provided a centrally hosted chatbot with RAG, but I also managed to get some surprisingly useful material using Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on my 24GB M2 MBA via a custom agent harness for Aleph/OpenAleph. [4]Happy to answer any questions about techy stuff, though I'm not a spokesperson for the project by any means. Seen a few people saying "just release the data!", but I think that slightly misunderstands what this work is. The whole point of forming a consortium of hundreds of journalists and sifting through the dump is to identify the bits that are in the public interest to report on -- especially important in jurisdictions like the UK, where I'm based, which have very strong defamation laws. Think Panama Papers, not Wikileaks.[1] https://darc.li/openaleph/ [2] https://followthemoney.tech/ [3] https://www.opensanctions.org/ [4] https://github.com/data-desk-eco/sift

articles.title: Multiple vulnerabilities in Regexp and String case conversion
articles.summary: Multiple vulnerabilities in Regexp and String case conversion

top_comments: There's what I think is probably an awesome bug here.Windows-1252 encoding has a representation for lowercase German sharp 's' (ß), but not one for the uppercase. If you upcase a string containing a sharp 's', it gets normalized to "SS", which increases the length of the string by one character. The 1252 case conversion code doesn't handle this; it looks like it checks for headroom in the buffer one character at a time. So if the last character of a string you upcase is ß, it looks like you get a one-byte overflow (of 'S').If that's really the bug (there's a claimed RCE POC), the heap grooming for it must be really fussy! I couldn't find any other character pairs that expand like this.You can feed strings in 1252 to a Rails program through multipart POSTs, which get to pick their encodings.The great thing about this bug, apart from how it illustrates how doomed we all are (if I'm right), is that it should by rights have the best vulnerability name of the year, because you get to work 'ß' into it.

str = ("\x82\xA0" + ("A" * (2**32 + 4))).force_encoding(Encoding::Shift_JIS) puts "str.bytesize: #{str.bytesize}" puts "str.encoding: #{str.encoding}" puts "str.valid_encoding?: #{str.valid_encoding?}" new_str = str.downcase puts "new_str.bytesize: #{new_str.bytesize}" puts "new_str.bytes: #{new_str.bytes}" puts "new_str.encoding: #{new_str.encoding}" outputs on an unfixed version: str.bytesize: 4294967302 str.encoding: Shift_JIS str.valid_encoding?: true new_str.bytesize: 6 new_str.bytes: [130, 160, 97, 97, 97, 97] new_str.encoding: Shift_JIS also I'd suggest you check out CVE-2026-128084 (GHSA-4fqr-96q8-xrfx) if you are interested in C bugs impacting Ruby on Rails
